The S.O.S. Band (sometimes written SOS Band; abbreviation for Sounds Of Success) is an American R&B and electro-funk group who gained fame in the 1980s. They are best known for the songs "Take Your Time (Do It Right)," "Just Be Good to Me," "Tell Me If You Still Care," and "The Finest." The band was founded in Atlanta, Georgia in 1977. The original group members included Willie "Sonny" Killebrew (saxophone), Billy Ellis (flute), Jason "T.C." Bryant (keyboards), Bruno Speight (guitar), John Simpson (bass), James Earl Jones III (drums), and Mary Davis (lead vocals, keyboards). It was originally known as Santa Monica, but later changed its name to The S.O.S. Band- an acronym for Sounds of Success. After listening to its demo and being impressed with their sound, Tabu Records founder Clarence Avant signed the group to its first recording contract. In 1980, the group released its first hit single, "Take Your Time (Do It Right)", which was certified platinum and sold over 2 million copies. Its debut album, S.O.S., went gold and sold over 800,000 copies. Trumpeter, vocalist, and percussionist Abdul Ra'oof joined the band while it was on a world tour. In 1983, the band joined forces with then-new production team of Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis, who went on to craft a string of R&B hits for the group, which included "Just Be Good to Me," "High Hopes," "Tell Me If You Still Care," "Borrowed Love," "No One's Gonna Love You," "Just the Way You Like It," and "The Finest." Lead vocalist Mary Davis left the group in 1987 to pursue a solo career, and was replaced by Chandra Currelley beginning with the band's 1989 Diamonds in the Raw album. They recorded another album with Currelley - 1991's One of Many Nights, which featured a few songs with a guest appearance from a then-unknown Kurupt. More recently, Currelley has been active as an actress and vocalist in Tyler Perry plays and movies. When Davis’s solo career was not as successful as she hoped, she reunited with the band in 1994. Since then, Davis spilt from the remaining members of The S.O.S. Band, with Davis and Speight both touring using the band's name with their versions of the current lineup. In 2013, The S.O.S. Band's entire Tabu Records catalog was reissued, as Tabu licensed their brand and trademark to British-based record label Demon Music Group. The Saint of Bleecker Street is a three-act opera with words and music by Gian Carlo Menotti. It was first performed at The Broadway Theatre in New York City on December 27, 1954. The Seasons (German: Die Jahreszeiten) is an oratorio by Joseph Haydn. An oratorio is a long musical work with orchestra, choir and solo singers. It usually tells a story from the Old Testament of the Bible. The Seasons is different. It is about the four seasons of the year. It describes nature and people's relationship to nature during the year. The Seasons was the last big work that Haydn composed. He composed it in 1801. By this time he was the most famous composer in Europe. Mozart had died ten years earlier, and Beethoven was a young man who was just starting to become famous. Haydn was nearly 80 years old and his health was not good. Although he lived another eight years The Seasons was the last big work he wrote. Soon after he had composed it he stopped composing altogether. Haydn had only written one big oratorio before The Seasons. This was an oratorio called The Creation. It had been performed in 1798 and was very popular all over Europe. The libretto (the words) had been written by Baron Gottfried van Swieten who was an Austrian nobleman who liked music. He had helped Mozart in his career and now he was helping Haydn. He wanted Haydn to write a second oratorio, so he wrote the libretto for The Seasons. He used a long English poem with the same title by James Thomson (1700-1748). He made it much shorter and changed it so that it was suitable to be set to music, and he translated it into German. Haydn took two years to write the music. It was first performed in Vienna on 24 April 1801. The audience liked it, although not as much as The Creation. One problem was that Haydn was not very happy about the libretto. He thought that oratorios should be about serious, dramatic stories from the Bible or from classical mythology, not about everyday life. Van Swieten was not very happy when Haydn criticized it, but he did not change it, and Haydn did his best to make the work interesting. The oratorio is divided into four parts, one for each of the seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. Each part lasts at least half an hour and consists of the usual recitatives (which tell the story), arias (songs), choruses (for the choir) and ensemble numbers (for the soloists together and often the chorus as well). There are three soloists (instead of the usual four). They represent three simple country people. There is a soprano called Hanne, a tenor called Lucas and a bass called Simon. Hanne is supposed to be Simon's daughter. There is no storyline in the normal sense: it is a series of poems and thoughts about nature during the year. The opening of Spring describes winter going away and spring awakening. There is a chorus which sounds very pastoral (like the countryside) with its 6/8 rhythm and drones (like country bagpipes). Simon then sings about the farmer sowing his seed. He is accompanied by a bassoon which sounds like a lively farmer tilling the earth. There is a gentle hymn of praise with a fugue which sounds like one from Mozart's Requiem. Hanne invites the girls and Simon invites the men to go to the fields and admire the earth, water and air. A chorus praises God. The music describes the countryside. The farmer is called to work in the morning (the oboe wakes him up). The sun rises. Again we thank God for nature. By midday it has become very hot. Later there are insects buzzing and we hear a shepherd playing on his pipe (the oboe). Everything is very dry at first, then there is a storm. The timpani make the sound of the thunder. When the storm has finished everyone is happy. We hear the birds singing, the frog croaking and the evening bell chimes eight times. The day's work is done. The words at first are about hard work and the rewards for hard work (Haydn thought these were strange words to set to music). Then there is a duet for a loving young couple (Lucas and Hanne). This is the only time that the soloists feel like real characters in a story and talk to one another. Autumn is the hunting season, so there is hunting music. It sounds quite old-fashioned (like Baroque music). The bassoon is the hound (the dog). The hounds become hungry and the music gets faster and faster until, suddenly, the dogs and the music stop. There is a gunshot (timpani) as the deer is shot. Autumn finishes with a drinking chorus. At first, there is thick winter fog. Then there is a short song (short because nothing grows in winter). Then there is a story about a traveller who is lost in the snow and comes to a cottage where he finds shelter. Hanne and the chorus sing a song about a spinning wheel. Many other composers later wrote music which describes a spinning wheel turning. There is another song which tells a story about a rich nobleman who tries to make love to a country girl but she escapes by riding off on his horse so he is left with no horse and no girl. At times this music sounds quite like the music in Mozart's opera The Magic Flute. Simon sings an aria which compares the seasons with the different stages of life (the seasons are used as a metaphor). Finally the chorus sing about the dawn of life in heaven. The oratorio and the seasons start all over again. The soloists, who have been three country people, are now three angels. There is a final hymn of praise.

"The Scientist" is the second single from British alternative rock band Coldplay's second album, A Rush of Blood to the Head. The song was written by all the band members for the album together. It is built around a piano ballad. Its lyrics tell the story about a man's desire to love and about an apology. The song was released in the United Kingdom as the second single from A Rush of Blood to the Head and reached number 10 in the UK Charts. It was released in the United States as the third single and reached number 18 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks. Critics praised "The Scientist". Several remixes of the track have been made. Its riff has been widely sampled. The single's music video won three MTV Music Video Awards, for the video's use of reverse narrative. The song was also featured on the band's 2003 live album Live 2003. On May 19, 2011, a cover of the song by Mike Posner was leaked. The song was used by WWE in a tribute to Macho Man Randy Savage that aired on Raw and Smackdown just a few days after his death on May 20, 2011. "The Scientist" is a melancholic, piano-driven ballad that was written in the key of F major. "1.36" features Tim Wheeler of Ash on guitar. "The Scientist" (video running backwards)

The Script are an Irish pop rock group from Dublin. They formed in 2001. They are currently based out of London. They are signed to the Sony Label Group. Their music has been featured in video games and popular TV programs. These have all gone to the top of the Irish charts. They also did really well in the UK charts, with the first two albums reaching number 1 and #3 reaching the second position. Their 2012 single Hall of Fame, made with will.i.am, was a worldwide success.

The Searchers were an English merseybeat band active in the 1960s. Their hit “Needles and Pins” was one of their successful song. Chris Curtis on drums, died after a long illness in 2005. Tony Jackson, died of liver cirrhosis in August 2003. John McNally lead singer, was born in 1941.

"The Seashores of Old Mexico" is a song by George Strait. The music video and premiered on March 23, 2006 on CMT. It debuted at number 20 on CMT's Top 20 Countdown for the week of April 20, 2006. The video peaked at number 1 on CMT's Top Twenty Countdown for two consecutive weeks in July 2006.

The Secret of Us is the second studio album by American singer-songwriter Gracie Abrams, released on June 21, 2024, by Interscope Records. It was mostly produced by Abrams and American musician Aaron Dessner. Two singles—"Risk" and "Close to You" came out before the album's release. "I Love You, I'm Sorry" was released as the third single months later. It became Abrams' first song to reach the top-20 region of the United States' Billboard Hot 100. American singer-songwriter Taylor Swift, appears on the track "Us" as a featured guest.

"The Secret Is Love" is a song recorded by Austrian singer Nadine Beiler. The song was released as a digital download on 3 January 2011 by Serious Entertainment as the lead single from her second studio album. The song was written by Nadine Beiler and produced by Thomas Rabitsch. It represented in the Eurovision Song Contest 2011 held in Düsseldorf, Germany. On 3 January 2011, Beiler was confirmed as one of thirty artists competing in Düsseldorf - wir kommen!, the Austrian national selection for the Eurovision Song Contest 2011, after ORF invited any interested artists to submit their songs between 26 October and 10 December 2010. The thirty songs were posted on Ö3's website for public voting between 3 and 31 January 2011. Ten entries were selected by a combination of public and jury vote to compete in the national final, the ten song were revealed on 1 February 2011, Beiler's song advanced to the national final. The national final took place on 25 February 2011, in the first round the top three songs were selected by a public vote to proceed to the second round, Beiler won the first round with 34.95% of the vote, she went on to win the second round winning the national final with 46.73% of the vote. At Eurovision, Austria competed in the second semi-final which took place on 12 May 2011, the song finished 7th with 69 points and advanced to the grand final which took place on 14 May 2011, the song finished 18th with 64 points.

The Shaggs were an American all-female rock group formed in Fremont, New Hampshire in 1968. The band was composed of sisters Dorothy "Dot" Wiggin (vocals/lead guitar), Betty Wiggin (vocals/rhythm guitar), Helen Wiggin (drums), and later Rachel Wiggin (bass). The sisters' father, Austin Wiggin, made Dot, Betty and Helen start a band. When Austin was young, his mother had predicted that Austin would have daughters who would be part of a famous music group. The band's only studio album, Philosophy of the World, was released in 1969. The album was not very well-known, though the band's live performances were popular in their local area. The Shaggs disbanded in 1975 after the death of Austin. Helen Wiggin died in 2006. The widow of Austin Wiggin, Jr., Annie Wiggin, died in 2005. The Shangri-Las were an American pop girl group of the 1960s. They released their first album Leader of the Pack in 1965. Their 1964 single "Leader of the Pack" was number one in the United States. The members of the group were sisters Betty and Mary Weiss, with twins, Margie and Mary-Ann Ganser. Their first hit recording was "Remember (Walking In The Sand)" (1964) which reached number 5 in the US and number 14 in the UK.

The Shadows were an English rock band active in the 1950s and 1960s. Their Former members were Hank Marvin Jet Harris Tony Meehan Cliff Richard and others. They were one of the successful rock groups in the 1960s.
The Shadows of Knight were an American rock band from Chicago, Illinois. They played a version of British blues inspired by Chicago. They began recording in 1965.

"The Shape I'm In" is a 1970 song by Canadian-American band The Band and was taken from their third studio album Stage Fright. It was the B-side to their single Time to Kill. It went to number 62 in Canada.

The Silence in Black and White is the first studio album by Hawthorne Heights. Victory Records released it on June 8, 2004. On Monday, June 27, 2005, the 2 disc special edition CD/DVD was released. The CD has acoustic versions of most of the songs. It also has a DVD containing live performances and many other features. Sean O'Keefe produced it. The album takes its title from a line in the song Niki FM. The album was number 56 on the Billboard 200 music chart. The Shirelles were a popular American girl group. They were very active from 1957 to 1982. Some of their songs were "I Met Him on a Sunday" and "Tonight's the Night". This group had four African American female singers. They had many hit records. The group broke apart in the very early 1980s. The group was formed by Shirley Owens (later Shirley Alston Reeves) who was the lead singer. At one time they had six songs in the Top Ten. Two of their songs, "Will You Love Me Tomorrow" (written by Carole King) and "Tonight's the Night", were selected by Rolling Stone on its list of the greatest songs of all time. Their song "soldier Boy" sold over five million copies.

"The Sign" is a hit song performed by Ace of Base. It was released as a single on 29 October 1993 in Europe. The song hit #2 on the UK Singles Chart. It spent six weeks near #1 in the United States. A cover version of this song was played on the television series Full House. Another version of this song lasts six minutes and 49 seconds.

"The Shock of the Lightning" is the first single off English rock band Oasis' seventh and final studio album Dig Out Your Soul. The song was released in 22 September 2008 as a download and on 29 September 2008 as a physical copy. Lead guitarist Noel Gallagher said of the song: "If 'The Shock of the Lightning" sounds instant and compelling to you, it's because it was written dead fast. And recorded dead fast. 'The Shock of the Lightning" basically is the demo. And it has retained its energy. And there's a lot to be said for that, I think. The first time you record something is always the best" NME ranked the song #96 on their list of 100 Tracks of the Decade.
The Shuffles were a Dutch pop band formed in Rosmalen, North Brabant. The group, fronted by the late Albert West, were active for ten years from 1963 until 1973.

"The Show Must Go On" is a 1991 song by the British rock band Queen and is the fifth and final single from their 14th studio album Innuendo. It went to number 2 in France, number 5 in Italy, number 6 in the Netherlands, number 7 in Germany and the Netherlands, number 11 in Switzerland, number 15 in Finland and number 16 in the United Kingdom.

The Signal (radio program), a Canadian radio program The Signal (Sandra Nasic album), the debut solo album of German singer Sandra Nasic The Signal (Urthboy album), the second album from The Herd member Urthboy "The Signal", a season-four episode of the British-American animated television series The Amazing World of Gumball The Santa Clarita Valley Signal, a news media organization in Santa Clarita, California The Signal (college newspaper), the official student newspaper of Georgia State University The Signal, The College of New Jersey's student-run newspaper since 1855

The Sick, the Dying... and the Dead! is the sixteenth studio album by American thrash metal band Megadeth. It was released by frontman Dave Mustaine's record label, Tradecraft, on September 2nd, 2022. It is the first album with drummer Dirk Verbeuren, and second album with guitarist Kiko Loureiro. While Megadeth was recording the album, bassist David Ellefson was fired from the band due to sexual videos of him being put on the internet. The bass recordings he made were taken off of the album, and replaced with recordings from Steve Di Giorgio, the bassist for Testament. The Sick, the Dying... and the Dead! took over two years to make. The band recorded the music for the album from 2019 to 2021. The release of the album was delayed many times. It was supposed to come out in 2019, but was released in September 2022 instead. In June 2019, the band cancelled many of the shows they were going to play at. This was because frontman Dave Mustaine had throat cancer. The band said they would keep making the album. In November 2018, Mustaine posted a few seconds of new music from the album on Twitter. At the time, the album was supposed to come out in 2019. The band went back to recording music for the album in 2020. It was now planned to be released in 2021. While talking to fans on Zoom, Mustaine said the album would be named The Sick, the Dying... and the Dead!. He also said that the band might change the album's name later. The band tried to release the album in early 2022, but had problems printing vinyl records. The album was finally released in September 2022.

"The Sidewinder Sleeps Tonite" is a 1993 song by alternative rock band R.E.M. and is the third single form their 8th studio album Automatic for the People. It is influenced by the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight. It went to number 1 in Iceland, number 13 in Ireland, number 17 in the United Kingdom and number 29 in New Zealand. It has never been played live in concerts. All songs were written by Bill Berry, Peter Buck, Mike Mills and Michael Stipe except as noted. The Silence in Black and White Acoustic is the sixth studio album by Hawthorne Heights. The album was released on April 15, 2014. It is a new version of their first studio album The Silence in Black and White with everything changed to acoustic.

"The Shelter of Your Eyes" is a 1972 debut single by Don Williams and is the leading single from his debut studio album Don Williams Volume One. It went to number 14 on the Billboard Hot Country Songs chart. It was covered by Charley Pride in 1973 and Lobo in 1975.

The Singles 1992-2003 is a greatest hits album by the American alternative rock band No Doubt. It was released on November 25, 2003 (the same day as Boom Box, a box set album by No Doubt.) The album contained all of the singles the band had released at the time, except for "Squeal" and "Doghouse" (two singles from their album The Beacon Street Collection that never became popular.) However, it also included two songs that were not singles: "Trapped in a Box" from their first album No Doubt, and a cover version of the song "It's My Life" by Talk Talk.

The Singles Collection is the second compilation album by Britney Spears. It was released in late 2009. It features the biggest hits of her career to that point plus one new song, "3", which was her first to debut at #1 on the Billboard Hot 100.

The Sisters of Mercy are an English gothic rock band that started in Leeds in 1980. They released their first album First and Last and Always in 1985, In 1987, they released their second album Floodland, In 1990, they released their third and final album Vision Thing. In 1990, they stopped making songs and albums because of disputes with their record label East West Records, from 1990 to the present day they perform new songs live. The Sisters of Mercy have been described as gothic rock, post-punk, dark wave and industrial rock. The Singing Dogs were a Danish musical recording project beginning during early-to-mid 1950s from recording engineer Carl Weismann and record producer Don Charles. (It is important, however, for this Don Charles to be not confused with the British recording artist and record producer under the same name.) The Singing Dogs names' were King, Dolly, Pussy, Pearl and Caesar. One of their most famous ballads is the classic song "Jingle Bells" (through which the dogs bark the lyrics).

The Singles: Echoes from the Edge of Heaven is the fourth compilation album by English pop duo Wham!. It was released in a variety of formats on 7 July 2023 by Sony Music in commemoration of the 40th anniversary of the duo's formation. The standard physical and digital version contains their singles in chronological order that were released from 1982 to 1986, along with several B-sides. An expanded digital version includes 17 additional tracks, made up of different mixes of the singles, which are included across the separate singles in the CD and seven-inch vinyl box sets. On 5 July 2023, a documentary film titled was released. In an interview with NME, Andrew Ridgeley said that he "really enjoyed the process of reviewing our career from this point of time and getting a sense of how much fun it was", calling being part of Wham! "almost exclusively a joyful and positive period in both our lives. It had a beginning, middle, and an end – so it makes a great story". "Go for It!" is an instrumental version of "Young Guns (Go for It!)". "Do It Right" is an instrumental version of "I'm Your Man".

The Smiths were an English rock band from Manchester. They formed in 1982 and split up in 1987. They released four studio albums. The band consisted of Morrissey (singing), Johnny Marr (guitar), Andy Rourke (bass) and Mike Joyce (drums). Critics have called them the most important alternative rock band to emerge from the British independent music scene of the 1980s. Q magazine writer Simon Goddard wrote that The Smiths were the one truly important group of the 1980s, "the most influential British guitar group of the decade" and the first independent group to become successful in the main music scene. The band was based on the songwriting partnership of Morrissey and Marr. They signed to the independent record label Rough Trade Records. On this, they released four studio albums: The Smiths (1984), Meat Is Murder (1985), The Queen Is Dead (1986) and Strangeways, Here We Come (1987). They have also released several compilations, and many singles that were not released on any of their studio albums. The Smiths had several singles reach the UK top twenty. All four of their albums reached the UK top five, including one which topped the charts. They won a large following of fans. The band had limited commercial success outside the UK while they were still together. The band broke up in 1987 and have refused several offers to reunite. The music focuses on a guitar, bass and drum sound. They blend 1960s rock and post-punk. This sounded very different to the synthesiser-based contemporary dance pop that was popular in the early 1980s. Marr's guitar playing on his Rickenbacker often had a jangly sound influenced by Roger McGuinn of the 1960s group The Byrds. It influenced later bands from Manchester, such as The Stone Roses and Oasis. Morrissey's lyrics combined stories about ordinary people's lives with a sense of humour.

The Slim Shady LP is the second studio album and the major-label debut by American rapper, Eminem. It was released on February 23, 1999 and was produced by Dr. Dre, Eminem, Mark & Jeff Bass, and Mel-Man. The album got critical and commercial success. It debuted at number two on the Billboard 200 charts. The first single from the album is "My Name Is". The Slits were a British punk band. The band was started in 1976. The members were Ari Up, Kate Korus, Suzy Gutsy, and Palmolive. In 1979 the band's first album Cut was released on Island Records in the UK. The band's second album was released in 1980. In 1982 the band broke up. The band got back together in 2005. It broke up again in 2010 when Ari Up died of cancer.

The Smiths is the self-titled first album by English rock band The Smiths. It was released on 20 February 1984 by Rough Trade Records. The album reached number two on the UK Albums Chart. It stayed on the chart for 33 weeks.

"The Song Is Over" is a song by English rock band The Who. It was on the album Who's Next. The band never performed the song live until March 30, 2025 at The Teenage Cancer Trust Concert at The Royal Albert Hall, London England..

The Song of Hiawatha is an epic poem written by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. It was first published in 1855. The poem was loosely based on the legends of Native American peoples. In 1857, Longfellow estimated that the work had sold 50,000 copies. The Song is about Hiawatha and his beloved Minnehaha. It is set along the south shore of Lake Superior. The poem was very popular, but critics did not like it. Composers and painters were inspired to create works based on the poem. A 2005 television movie was based on the poem. Hiawatha's birth is foretold by a "mighty" peace-bringing leader named Gitche Manito. A woman named Nokomis falls from the moon. Nokomis gives birth to Wenonah. She grows to be a beautiful young woman. Nokomis warns her not to be seduced by the West Wind. She does not listen to her mother, and Hiawatha is born. Hiawatha has childhood adventures, falls in love with Minnehaha, slays the evil magician Pearl-Feather, invents written language, discovers corn, and other episodes. The poem closes with the approach of a canoe to Hiawatha's village. It contains "the Priest of Prayer, the Pale-face." Hiawatha welcomes him with joy. The "Black-Robe chief" brings word of Jesus Christ. Hiawatha and the chiefs accept the Christian message. Hiawatha says good-bye to Nokomis, the warriors, and the young men. He says, "But my guests I leave behind me / Listen to their words of wisdom, / Listen to the truth they tell you." He endorses the Christian missionaries. He launches his canoe for the last time westward toward the sunset. Then he departs forever.

The Sorcerer is an operetta by Gilbert and Sullivan. It is the third of their fourteen operettas. It opened in London at the Opera Comique on 17 November 1877. It ran for 178 performances. The play is about the effects of a love potion on the residents of an English village.

The Soul Sessions is the debut studio album by English singer-songwriter Joss Stone. It was released on 16 September 2003 by S-Curve Records and EMI/Virgin Records. When The Soul Sessions was released on 16 September 2003. At the time Stone was just 16 years old. The album took four days to record. The songs on the album are cover versions of classic soul songs. The Soul Sessions received positive reviews from music critics.

The Soul Sessions Vol. 2 is the sixth studio album by English singer-songwriter Joss Stone, released on 20 July 2012 by S-Curve Records and her own label, Stone'd Records. Like her debut album The Soul Sessions (2003) where the songs were covers of classic soul songs, The Soul Sessions Vol. 2s songs are covers of soul and R&B songs that were originally made during the 1970s. The Soul Sessions Vol. 2 received positive reviews from music critics.

The Song of Roland is an epic poem in Old French. It tells the story of a battle in the Pyrenees in 778, during the reign of Charlemagne. It is the oldest surviving chanson de geste, and one of the oldest important works of French literature. A few shorter religious poems in Old French, such as the Sequence of Saint Eulalia (about 880) and the Life of Saint Alexis (about 1050), are older. The version people usually mean is the one kept in a manuscript in Oxford. It has just over 4,000 lines. Most scholars think it was written around the year 1100, near the time of the First Crusade. The last line of the poem names a man called Turoldus, but nobody knows who he was, or even what his part in the poem was. The poem is based on history, but changes it greatly. In the Frankish accounts, Basques attack Charlemagne's rearguard. In the poem, the enemies are Muslim Saracens, and the defeat becomes part of a holy war between Christians and "pagans". The poem is written in lines of ten syllables. There is usually a pause after the fourth syllable, which splits each line into two parts of four and six syllables. The lines are grouped into laisses, which are stanzas of uneven length. Lines in a laisse do not rhyme. Instead they all end on the same stressed vowel sound, which is called assonance. Editors usually number 4,002 lines, although only 3,998 are actually written in the Oxford manuscript. Two pairs of lines were run together by the copyist, and a few lines are missing. Editors also divide the text into laisses in different ways. Most modern editors count 291 laisses, but Whitehead counts 298. The poet often tells the same moment two or three times in a row, changing small details each time. Scholars call these laisses similaires. He also uses set phrases that fit exactly into half a line. These habits probably come from traditions of oral poetry. The poem was meant to be heard rather than read silently. It may have been sung, recited, or read aloud, and jongleurs, who were travelling performers, probably performed versions of the story. The letters "AOI" appear 180 times in the Oxford manuscript, and in no other copy. They usually come at the end of a laisse, but 21 times they appear elsewhere, and many laisses do not have them at all. Scholars have suggested that they mark a musical refrain, or a note to the singer or the copyist, or a short form of a word such as "amen". Nobody knows. Charlemagne has fought in Spain for seven years. He has taken every city except Saragossa, which is held by King Marsile. Marsile cannot beat the Franks in battle. On the advice of Blancandrin, he offers Charlemagne treasure and hostages, and promises to come to Aix and become a Christian. He does not mean to keep the promise. The Frankish barons argue. Roland, the emperor's nephew, says Marsile cannot be trusted, and reminds them that two earlier envoys were killed. Ganelon, who is Roland's stepfather, says the war should end. Charlemagne decides to send a messenger, and Roland proposes Ganelon. Ganelon takes this as an attempt to have him killed. He tells Roland in front of the whole court that he will get his revenge. At Saragossa, Ganelon makes a deal with Marsile. He will arrange for Roland to command the rearguard when the army goes home, and Marsile will attack it in the mountains. Ganelon then returns with gifts and false promises, and names Roland for the rearguard. Roland takes with him Oliver, Archbishop Turpin, the rest of the twelve peers, and 20,000 men. A very large Saracen force attacks the rearguard at Rencesvals. Oliver sees the enemy and asks Roland to blow his horn, the oliphant, so that Charlemagne will turn back. Roland refuses. He says it would bring shame on him and on his family. The poet tells this famous scene in three similar laisses. The French kill great numbers of the enemy, but they are far too few. When almost all his men are dead, Roland decides to blow the horn. Oliver now says it is too late, and blames Roland for the deaths. Turpin makes peace between the two friends. Roland blows so hard that his temples burst. Charlemagne hears the sound far away and turns back, and Ganelon is arrested. Roland cuts off Marsile's right hand with his sword, Durendal, and Marsile flees. Oliver is struck from behind and dies. Turpin is wounded again and again, but keeps fighting beside Roland. Then the Saracens hear the trumpets of Charlemagne's returning army. They do not dare come close to Roland, so they throw their spears at him from a distance, kill his horse Veillantif, and run away. Roland is left on foot, alone with the dying archbishop. He binds Turpin's wounds and lays him on the grass, then gathers the bodies of Oliver and the peers so that Turpin can bless them. Turpin dies soon afterwards, while trying to fetch water for Roland. Roland tries to break Durendal on a rock so that no pagan can use it, but the sword will not break. He lies down under a pine tree with his face turned towards Spain, so that people will know he died attacking. He confesses his sins and holds out his right glove to God. The archangel Gabriel takes the glove, and angels carry his soul to heaven. Charlemagne reaches the battlefield and finds the dead. He prays, and God stops the sun so that the day will last longer. The Franks catch the fleeing Saracens and drive them into the river Ebro, where they drown. Baligant, an emir who brings a huge fleet from Egypt, then arrives to help Marsile. There is a second great battle, and Charlemagne kills Baligant in single combat. The Franks take Saragossa. Marsile dies, and his queen Bramimonde is taken prisoner. The bodies of Roland, Oliver and Turpin are carried back to Blaye. At Aix, Aude, who is Oliver's sister and Roland's promised wife, asks where Roland is. When Charlemagne tells her he is dead, she falls at his feet and dies. Ganelon is then put on trial. He argues that he was not a traitor, because he had openly challenged Roland before the court, so his revenge was lawful. His powerful kinsman Pinabel offers to fight anyone who votes against him. The barons are afraid and ask Charlemagne to let Ganelon go. Only one knight, Thierry, disagrees. Thierry and Pinabel fight a judicial duel, which was believed to show God's judgment, and Thierry wins. Ganelon is torn apart by four horses, and thirty of his relatives are hanged. Bramimonde becomes a Christian and is baptised Juliana. That night Gabriel tells Charlemagne to set out again and help Christians in another land, and the old emperor weeps. The best-known line in the poem says that Roland is proz and Oliver is sage. This is often translated "Roland is brave and Oliver is wise", and readers have long treated it as a contrast between two kinds of hero. Other scholars disagree. They point out that the poet joins the two halves with "and", not "but", and that proz means something closer to "worthy" than to "brave". On that reading the line says the two friends are equal, not opposite. The quarrel over the horn lies behind this debate. Oliver tells Roland that bravery is not the same as folly, that self-control is better than rashness, and that Frenchmen have died because of his recklessness. But Oliver says this in the middle of a lost battle, and it is not clear that the poet agrees with him. Ganelon also calls Roland proud, and Ganelon is a liar. Some critics read Roland as a tragic hero destroyed by his own fault; others read him as a martyr who chooses to die for a cause. The poem does not settle the question. Ganelon never denies that he took revenge on Roland. He argues that he had challenged Roland openly in front of the court, so what followed was lawful revenge and not treason. How treason should be defined was a real and difficult legal question in the poet's own day. The barons cannot answer it, and they are too frightened of Pinabel to try. In the end the case is settled not by argument but by a duel, which the poem treats as the judgment of God. Roland states plainly that the pagans are wrong and the Christians are right. Yet the poet builds the two sides in the same shape. Each opens with a king taking counsel from his barons. Each has twelve peers. Both are feudal societies with the same ideas of honour and service. The poet gives the Saracens three gods, Mahomet, Tervagan and Apollo. This looks like a copy of the Christian Trinity, but it does not describe real Islam, which is a religion of one God. Recent critics have paid close attention to this mixture of sharp opposition and close likeness. Scholars also disagree about what drives the poem as a whole. Some read it as a work of the crusading age, in which death fighting "pagans" is a kind of martyrdom. Others see an older warrior code of honour and loyalty between lord and vassal, with Christian language laid over it. Many now think the poem holds both together. In 778 Charlemagne led an army into Spain. He had been invited by Sulayman al-Arabi, a Muslim governor who had rebelled against the ruler of Córdoba. Charlemagne besieged Saragossa, but the city was not handed over. News of a Saxon revolt at home forced him to give up the siege. He took hostages, including Sulayman, and fell back to Pamplona, whose walls he destroyed. On 15 August 778 the army crossed the Pyrenees in a long column through a narrow pass. Attackers who were waiting at the top fell on the baggage train and the rearguard. The Franks were slowed by the ground and by their heavy armour. They were killed, the baggage was taken, and the attackers scattered under cover of night. Charlemagne could not punish them, because they could not be found. The Frankish annals said nothing about the defeat while Charlemagne was alive. A later version of the royal annals mentions an ambush by Basques but gives no names. Around 830, Einhard wrote in his Life of Charlemagne that three important men were killed: Eggihard, the head of the royal table; Anselm, count of the palace; and Hruodland, prefect of the Breton March. Roland is named last, and his name is missing from some copies of the text. The exact date of the battle is known from the tomb inscription of Eggihard. Later Arab historians tell a different story. Ibn al-Athir, writing in the 13th century, says that Sulayman changed sides, that Charlemagne seized him and carried him off as a prisoner, and that Sulayman's sons attacked the Franks in the pass and freed their father, probably with Basque help. If this is right, Rencesvals was not simply a raid on the baggage by mountain villagers, but a real defeat at the hands of Muslim forces. Ian Short treats this as a possible reconstruction rather than a proven fact. Whether Roland himself existed is also debated. Besides Einhard, his name appears on Carolingian coins in the form Rodlan and in a charter of 772, but nothing else is known about him. Between 778 and about 1100 the story changed in several ways: The Basques become Saracens, so a mountain defeat becomes a war of religion. Charlemagne's few months in Spain become seven years. Roland becomes Charlemagne's nephew and the first of his twelve peers, instead of one name in a list of the dead. The defeat is caused by treason inside the Frankish camp, and is fully avenged. There is evidence that the story was already well known before the poem was written. From the early 11th century, pairs of brothers across western Europe were often named Roland and Oliver. A short Latin note written in Spain, the Nota Emilianense, already says that Charlemagne's men died at Rencesvals at the hands of Saracens. The Oxford version is in a single manuscript in the Bodleian Library, known as Digby 23. It was copied in England, roughly between 1125 and 1150, in Anglo-Norman, the French spoken by the ruling class in England after the Norman conquest. The same book also contains a Latin translation of Plato's Timaeus. The copyist made many small mistakes, but he did not try to improve the text, which is one reason it is valued. A second scribe later went through the book and altered some readings, often for the worse. Six other substantial French manuscript versions survive, as well as some fragments, such as the Lorraine fragments and the fragments published by Lavergne. None of them comes from the Oxford text; they come from a similar but different version. They were copied between the middle of the 13th century and the early 15th century. Three are from France and three from Italy. Some of them replace the assonance with full rhyme, and most add long new passages, especially about Ganelon and about Aude. Scholars have usually given the Oxford version a special place, because it is the earliest surviving French version and has a distinctive poetic style. Seven manuscripts is not a large number for a medieval poem. The Romance of the Rose, for example, survives in more than 300. The story itself, however, was clearly popular, and it was retold in other languages: in German (the Rolandslied of Konrad, about 1131 to 1133), in Old Norse (part of the Karlamagnús saga, about 1230 to 1250), and in Welsh, English and Dutch. The Oxford manuscript has no title. The name La Chanson de Roland was given to it by Francisque Michel, who published the first printed edition in 1837. The Oxford poem is usually dated to about 1100, but this is not certain. Scholars have argued for dates from the first half of the 11th century to the second half of the 12th. The handwriting of the manuscript has been dated in different ways too, from about 1125 to about 1170. The last line of the poem reads: Ci falt la geste que Turoldus declinet. It can be translated as "Here ends the tale that Turoldus tells", but almost every word is debated. It is not clear whether "the tale" means the poem, the source the poet used, or the copy the scribe was working from. The verb declinet has been translated as "composes", "copies", "recites" and "makes known". So Turoldus may have been the poet, a scribe, or a performer. Turold is a common Norman name of Scandinavian origin, and several real men of that name have been suggested, but none can be proved. A figure with the name Turold written above him even appears on the Bayeux Tapestry. Some scholars have tried to link him with the Turoldus of the poem, but no link can be shown. In the 19th and early 20th centuries scholars argued about whether the poem was the work of one gifted poet, or the last stage of centuries of oral storytelling. Most scholars today take a middle view: an old story shaped by oral tradition was given careful literary form by one poet, who used the techniques of oral poetry so that the work would sound well when read aloud. Roland – Charlemagne's nephew and the first of the twelve peers. His sword is Durendal, his horn is the oliphant and his horse is Veillantif. Oliver – Roland's closest companion and Aude's brother. He is careful where Roland is bold. Turpin – the archbishop who fights beside them and blesses the dying. Charlemagne – the emperor. In the poem, Saracen speakers say that he is more than two hundred years old. Ganelon – Roland's stepfather, who betrays the rearguard. Pinabel – Ganelon's kinsman, who fights for him in the judicial duel. Thierry – the knight who accuses Ganelon and wins the duel. Naimon – Charlemagne's wisest counsellor. Aude – Oliver's sister and Roland's promised wife. King Marsile – the Saracen king of Saragossa. Blancandrin – Marsile's clever counsellor. Bramimonde – Marsile's queen, and the only important Saracen figure who survives the final defeat. Baligant – the emir who comes from the East to help Marsile. The pilgrim roads to Santiago de Compostela may have helped the stories about Roland to spread. A Latin chronicle of about 1140, wrongly said to be by Archbishop Turpin himself, retells the legend and was widely read; the stained glass windows of Chartres Cathedral follow that version. Roland was also carved in stone at Verona cathedral, and the town of Blaye grew as the supposed burial place of Roland and Oliver. Around 1125, William of Malmesbury wrote that a song about Roland was sung to the Norman troops before the Battle of Hastings. The Norman poet Wace later named the singer as Taillefer, and said he sang of Charlemagne, Roland, Oliver and the men who died at Rencesvals. In Italy, Roland became Orlando. He is the hero of two famous Renaissance poems, Orlando Innamorato by Matteo Maria Boiardo and Orlando Furioso by Ludovico Ariosto. There are also two Occitan poems about him, Ronsasvals and Roland à Saragosse. In the 19th and early 20th centuries the poem was treated in France as a national epic. Gaston Paris gave public readings of it during the siege of Paris in 1870, and Joseph Bédier borrowed its language for French government pamphlets during the First World War. Later critics have been much less interested in this patriotic reading.

Ziggy's 'life' came to an end in a live concert at the Hammersmith Odeon on July 3, 1973. This show was released as a movie in 1983, called Ziggy Stardust - The Motion Picture. The Specials were an English new wave/ska band. They were originally from Coventry, England and formed in 1977. They were part of the ska revival in Britain in the late 1970s and early 1980s. During the ska revival, bands began playing 1960s-style Jamaican ska music. The Specials often mixed other popular music styles from the 1970s and 1980s into their music, such as punk rock.

"The Spirit of Radio" is a 1980 song by Canadian progressive rock band Rush. It is the leading single from their seventh studio album Permanent Waves and went to number 51 in the United States, number 13 in the United Kingdom and number 22 in Canada. It has became one of their best known singles and was a concert staple.

"The Sound of Silence" (originally "The Sounds of Silence") is a 1964 debut single by Simon & Garfunkel and is the leading single from their debut studio album Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M.. It went to number 1 in the United States, Japan and South Africa, number 2 in New Zealand, number 3 in Zimbabwe, Australia and Austria, number 10 in the Netherlands and number 4 in Canada. It was covered by Paul Simon in 1974. In 2015, it was covered by American alternative band Disturbed for their sixth studio album Immortalized. It went to number 42 in the United States, number 4 in Australia, number 29 in the United Kingdom, number 31 in Ireland, number 32 in New Zealand and number 1 in Austria.

"The Space Between" is a 2001 song by Dave Matthews Band and is the second single from their fourth studio album Everyday. It went to number 22 in the United States, number 36 in the United Kingdom, number 25 in Scotland, number 97 in Australia and number 69 in the Netherlands.

They officially formed The Starlings in 2018.

"The Story of Us" is a song written and recorded by American singer-songwriter Taylor Swift. The song was produced by Nathan Chapman and Swift. It is about breakups and troubles between two people. The story in the song was inspired by an encounter with an ex-boyfriend during the CMT Music Awards in which Swift and the ex attempted to ignore one another. "The Story of Us" received mixed reviews, peaking at #41 on Billboard Hot 100, although the video got positive review for its "departure from the music video high school". The song was on Swift's album Speak Now, released in 2010.

The Stone Roses are an English rock band fronted by Ian Brown. It was started in Manchester in 1983. In 1989 the band released their first album The Stone Roses. Seven singles were released from the album which went on to be voted the best British album of all time. In 1994 the band released their second album, Second Coming. In 1996 the band broke up. The band got back together in 2011. On May 21, 2012 the band announced a reunion tour and performed for the first time in 16 years. In 2013 a documentary called The Stone Roses: Made of Stone was released. The band split up for a second time in 2017.

The Stooges are an American protopunk band. They were formed in 1967 in Ann Arbor, Michigan and began to record music two years later. Their first album was released in August 1969. It was produced by John Cale from The Velvet Underground. They released two more albums before the first members broke up in 1974. The Stooges's music has been described as Protopunk, garage rock, hard rock, punk rock and heavy metal. Iggy Pop and their members singing just like MC5, Dr. Feelgood and New York Dolls.

"The Story in Your Eyes" is a 1971 song by English progressive rock band The Moody Blues and was taken from their seventh studio album Every Good Boy Deserves Favour. It went to number 23 in the United States and number 7 in Canada.

The Strokes are an American band formed in 1998. They became famous in the early 2000s as a leading group in the garage rock revival. The members of the band are Julian Casablancas, Nick Valensi, Albert Hammond Jr., Nikolai Fraiture and Fabrizio Moretti. The band has released six studio albums, but their first album, Is This It is their most famous. Casablancas, Moretti and Valensi were the first members of the band and started playing together when they were still in high school. In 1998, Hammond joined the band. They spent two years playing live in New York City, but no one really listened to them. They recorded some songs and sent them to record labels, but their offers were not accepted. On October 2000, the band went to Gordon Raphael's studio and recorded songs, but with no extra effects. Rough Trade Records founder Geoff Travis found out the songs and released them as The Modern Age EP. The Strokes were also featured in a famous magazine, the NME. Because of these, the band was noticed by a lot of people, but most of those people were in the UK.

The Streets are an rap/garage band whose lead singer, multi-instrumentalist & record producer was Mike Skinner, a British rapper. Born in Birmingham, Skinner has often been criticised for using a mockney accent during interviews and in many songs. They released their first album, "Original Pirate Material", in 2002, The album's singles were "Has It Come To This", "Let's Push Things Forward", "Don't Mug Yourself", "The Irony Of It All" and "Weak Become Heroes. His next album, called "A Grand Don't Come For Free" came out in 2004 and is their most successful album. All the songs on the album help tell a story about a man with a broken TV who lost £1000, with other things happening while trying to get the TV repaired. The album includes his most successful singles "Fit But You Know It" and "Dry Your Eyes" which became number 1 in the charts. And the reunion in 2017.

The Sufferer & the Witness is the fourth album by American punk rock band Rise Against. The album was released on July 4, 2006. It was their second release on popular label, Geffen Records. The album follows 2004's Siren Song of the Counter Culture. It sold 48,000 copies in its first week, debuting at number 10 on the Billboard 200. It has been awarded Gold by the RIAA. The song "Drones" was used for WWE's 2007 Royal Rumble's theme song. After the good reviews of their big label debut, Siren Song of the Counter Culture, and its single, "Swing Life Away", Rise Against came back to the studio in January 2006 to start their fourth studio album. The band had been writing songs and ideas during the Siren Song of the Counter Culture tour and had finished five songs by early December 2005. Also in December, it was said that Bill Stevenson would make the album at the Blasting Room studio in Fort Collins, Colorado. The band began in January 2006 in Chicago. It was made with Bill Stevenson and Jason Livermore for 12 weeks between January and April 2006. The band talked about the sound and release date of the album in April, saying, "We're pretty excited and can't wait for you to hear it. You won't find any acoustic guitar on this one, but perhaps a few other surprises and curveballs await your curious ears...look for an early summer release." The album's name was told in the same news release. It would be called The Sufferer & the Witness. The album was mixed by Chris Lord-Alge in Los Angeles. It was finished in April 2006.

The Sugarhill Gang is an American hip hop group. They are best known for their 1979 single "Rapper's Delight". It was the first hip hop song to enter the top 40 in the United States. The song was on their first album Sugarhill Gang. The group formed in 1973. They broke up in 2007. They have released four studio albums.

"The Stranger" is a 1978 song by Billy Joel and is the title track from his fifth studio album of the same name. It went to number 2 in Japan, number 8 in New Zealand and number 59 in Australia and France. It was not released in the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada and Ireland.

The Subways are an English rock band. They are from Welwyn Garden City, Hertfordshire. They were formed in 2002. It consists of Billy Lunn, Charlotte Cooper, and Camille Phillips. The band's name comes from a time when brothers Billy Lunn and Josh Morgan and Charlotte Cooper used to hang around the local subway underpass which ran underneath a Welwyn Garden City roundabout.

The Stunners were an American girl group formed in Los Angeles in 2007. Originally the members were Allie Gonino, Hayley Kiyoko, Marisol Esparza, Kelsey Sanders, and Tinashe. In July 2009 after the debut single "Bubblegum", Sanders left the group and was replaced by Lauren Hudson. The group disbanded in 2011.

The Sweet (also known as Sweet) are a British glam rock band. The group is famous for the songs such as "Ballroom Blitz", "Little Willy", "Fox on the Run" and "Love is Like Oxygen". The group was originally called Sweetshop.

The Swell Season are an Academy Award winning folk rock duo. The members are Glen Hansard and Marketa Irglova. Hansard is a member of the Irish band The Frames. Irglova is a classically trained Czech pianist and singer. The duo won the Academy Award for Best Song in 2008. The Swell Session made their first album, The Swell Season, in 2006. It was just after the release of the Frames' sixth CD, The Cost. Hansard and Irglová also appeared as working-class immigrants in the popular Irish movie, Once. The movie was shown at the Sundance Film Festival in 2007. The next year, they won the Academy Award for Best Song for the song "Falling Slowly" from that movie. Hansard is the first Irish-born person to win in that category. Irglová is the first Czech woman to win an Oscar. At age 19, she became the youngest person to win an Oscar in a musical category. The soundtrack, Once: Music from the Motion Picture, was certified as gold in February 2008. They went on tour and performed to sold-out crowds in many countries. Hansard and Irglová also recorded a version of Bob Dylan's "You Ain't Goin' Nowhere" for the movie I'm Not There in 2007. During the tour, Hansard and Irglová began dating. Hansard said, "I had been falling in love with her for a long time, but I kept telling myself she's just a kid". In 2009, Hansard said that he and Irglova were no longer romantically linked, and that they are now "good friends." Hansard and Irglová performed "Falling Slowly" live on the Oscar broadcast at Los Angeles' Kodak Theater on February 24, 2008. When they went on stage to receive their awards, Irglova's acceptance speech was stopped by the orchestra's music cue to leave the stage. Host Jon Stewart asked her back to give her speech after the commercial break. Ceremony director Gil Cates said the early cue was an accident.

The Sundays were an English alternative rock band. They formed in the late 1980s. They released three albums in the 1990s. The band started when Harriet Wheeler and guitarist David Gavurin met. The Sundays got a record deal with the Rough Trade Records. Their first single, "Can't be Sure", was released in 1989. Their first album, Reading, Writing and Arithmetic, was released in 1990. The album got very positive reviews. It entered the UK chart at #4. Later in 1990, the album peaked at #39 in the United States. Its success came mostly from radio stations playing "Here's Where the Story Ends". In late October 1992, the next album, Blind, was released. This album was also successful when it peaked at #103 on the Billboard 200. Blind sold half a million copies. The reviews were positive. Some critics thought the album didn't have the quality songwriting of the first album. In autumn 1997, after five years, their third record, Static & Silence, was released. It got mixed reviews. "Summertime", the first song on the album, was their most successful song the UK Charts up to that time. The Sundays took a break after the album Static & Silence.

The Swinging Laurels are an English synth-pop and new wave band formed in Leicester during 1979. The band was created by saxophonists Gary "Gaz" Birtles and John Barrow. Their debut single, "Peace of Mind", topped the independent charts in 1981. Over the next decade, the band members also worked as session horn players for popular British acts, including Fun Boy Three and Culture Club. Gaz Birtles originally sang in a Leicester ska band called The Newmatics, while John Barrow played saxophone for the funk group Black Gorilla. By 1979, the two musicians started writing music together using an Elgam organ drum machine, a Roland synthesizer, and a tape recorder. This setup allowed them to combine synth rhythms with sax melodies. To take their project on stage, they brought in extra members: drummer Nick Murphy from The Newmatics, trumpeter Dean Sargent, and keyboard player Mark O'Hara. The group recorded their first single "Peace of Mind" at Woodbine Street Studios, which reached number one on the Melody Maker Independent Chart in 1981. By mid-1982, the band was invited to perform a live radio session for John Peel on BBC Radio 1. Around the same time, other artists began hiring their brass section. They recorded horns for Fun Boy Three's single "The Telephone Always Rings" and appeared alongside them on Top of the Pops. Impressed by their sound, Boy George asked the group to support Culture Club on two major UK concert tours in 1983. The Swinging Laurels signed with WEA Records in 1982 and put out the single "Rodeo". A year later, they released "Lonely Boy", produced by Steve Levine. Although Boy George sang backing vocals on "Lonely Boy", his main label Virgin Records blocked the release due to contract rules. The group had to wipe his vocals from the final mix, which hurt sales and led WEA to cancel their planned studio album. After leaving WEA in 1984, the band set up their own label, Happy Records, and issued the single "Zoom (Take the Test)". They briefly renamed themselves Happy House in 1985 while performing with singer Rhoda Dakar. Birtles and Barrow later joined the rock band Crazyhead as a horn section, backing Iggy Pop on a 1988 European tour. The Swinging Laurels officially broke up in 1989. Following the split, Birtles toured as a saxophonist with The Beautiful South, while Barrow did session work for artists such as Suggs and Sinéad O'Connor. The band briefly reunited in 1997. Decades later, in May 2024, Birtles and Barrow gathered their old 1980s tapes and released their first full-length album, Return to the Future, through Scatola Rosa. "The Take Over, The Breaks Over" (the quotes are a part of the name) is a 2007 song by the band Fall Out Boy. It was released in 2007 on their album Infinity on High. The video focuses on Pete Wentz's dog, Hemmingway. The video, which was made in black and white, shows Hemmingway in a dream.

The System Has Failed is the tenth studio album by American thrash metal band Megadeth. It was released on September 14, 2004 by Sanctuary Records. It was the band's first album after frontman Dave Mustaine's arm injury. It is also the first Megadeth album to not have bassist David Ellefson playing on it. Critics liked The System Has Failed, and it came out at number 18 on the Billboard 200 charts. Many thought that the album sounded more like heavy metal than the band's previous albums, like Risk. "Die Dead Enough" and "Of Mice and Men" were released as singles in 2004. "The Scorpion" was also released as a single in 2005.

The Sword was an American heavy metal band from Austin, Texas. It was made in 2003 by singer and guitarist John Cronise, guitarist Kyle Shutt, and drummer Trivett Wingo. The band released their first album, Age of Winters, in 2006. Cronise had written most of the album's music before making the band. Two years later, the band made Gods of the Earth, which reached number 102 on the Billboard 200 music chart. In 2010, the band released Warp Riders. This was a concept album based on a science fiction story that Cronise made. Drummer Trivett Wingo left the band, and was replaced by Santiago Vega. After signing with a new record label, Razor & Tie, the band made three more albums: Apocryphon in 2012, High Country in 2015, and Used Future in 2018. The band ended in October 2022. When they were first making music, people called The Sword a doom metal band. Members of the band said they were inspired by other bands, such as Sleep and Black Sabbath. Later, people said the band's music sounded more like hard rock and stoner rock. The Sword has toured with many other metal bands, such as Lamb of God, Metallica, and Clutch.

The Turn of the Screw is an opera by Benjamin Britten. It is a chamber opera (an opera for a small number of characters and very small orchestra). The story is based on a story with the same title by Henry James. The libretto (the words of the opera) were written by Myfanwy Piper. The story of the opera is almost exactly the same as in Henry James’s book. Britten was asked by the Venice Biennale to write the opera. It was first performed on 14 September, 1954, at the Teatro La Fenice, Venice. Its first performance in Britain took place a month later on 6 October 1954 at Sadler’s Wells Opera in London. The opera is divided into two acts. It is further divided into a prologue and sixteen scenes. Before each scene starts we hear a variation on the 'Screw' theme. This theme is based on twelve notes which are all the 12 notes in the octave. This is called twelve-tone row, but it is tonally based (the music is in traditional keys, unlike the music of Schoenberg). There are only 13 players in the orchestra. Time: The middle of the nineteenth century The prologue is just for a solo singer (tenor) and piano. He tells us about a young governess he once knew who looked after two children at Bly House. The children’s parents were dead, and they were supposed to be cared for by their uncle. The uncle, who lived in London, was far too busy to care for them, and he hired a governess for them. He told the governess (who is just called “the governess” in the opera) that she must never write to him about the children. She must make any decisions about them herself. She must never ask him about the history of Bly House, and she must always continue to care for the children. The Governess wonders what the children will be like. The children wonder what their new governess will be like. When the Governess arrives at Bly House she is greeted by the housekeeper, Mrs. Grose, and the children who (bow and curtsey). She thinks that the boy, Miles, looks strangely familiar. Miles goes to a boarding school, but he has come home for the holidays. A letter from his school arrives saying that he has been expelled because he had been threatening other children. The Governess is sure that Miles, like his sister Flora, is too kind and innocent to have done such terrible things. Mrs Grose also thinks the same thing. The Governess decides not to take any notice of the letter. The Governess sings about her wonderful position at the house and the beautiful children she has in her care. But at night she hears strange footsteps and a cry outside her door. Suddenly, she sees a pale-faced man sitting on a tower of the house. When the man disappears, she becomes frightened and wonders if she has seen a ghost. But then she is comforted when she hears the children singing the nursery rhyme "Tom, Tom, the Piper's Son". The Governess doubts that she saw anything, but decides to tell Mrs. Grose. The housekeeper tells the Governess about Peter Quint, who used to be a servant at Bly House. What Mrs. Grose says seems to suggest that Quint had done nasty things to Miles. At that time Miles had a governess called Miss Jessel. Mrs. Grose suggests that Quint had a sexual relationship with Miss Jessell, and that they both had sexual relations with the children. The housekeeper said she could do nothing about it, as Quint cleverly found any letters that came for her and he threatened her with physical harm. But when Miss Jessel became pregnant and people found out how bad she was, she abandoned the children and ran away. Soon afterwards she died. Shortly after that Quint died a mysterious death on an icy road near Bly House. The next morning, the Governess is teaching Miles Latin when he goes into a trance-like state and sings a song which shows that Quint had abused him. Later that day, the Governess sits by the side of a lake with Flora. Flora names the seas of the world, finishing with the Dead Sea. Flora compares the Dead Sea (where nothing can live) to Bly House. This worries the Governess. As Flora plays on the shore with her doll, the Governess suddenly sees a strange woman across the lake who seems to be watching Flora. It is the ghost of Miss Jessel, who has returned to get Flora. The Governess hurries Flora home to safety. That night, Miles and Flora slip out into the woods to meet Miss Jessel and Peter Quint. The children fantasize about a world where dreams come true. The Governess and Mrs. Grose arrive as the children are about to be possessed, and the spirits depart. Miles sings a song about how he has been a bad boy. The ghosts of Peter Quint and Miss Jessel reappear. They argue about who harmed whom first when they were alive, and accuse one another of not acting quickly enough to possess the children. In her room, the Governess worries about the evil she feels in the house. The next morning, the family goes to church. The children sing a song which sounds like a song praising God. Mrs. Grose does not realize the meaning of the song until the Governess tells her they are singing about horrors. The Governess runs off and goes to her room. She can feel the presence of Miss Jessel and sees her sitting at her desk. The Governess now knows that she cannot abandon the children. She writes to the children’s uncles saying that she must see him. When the Governess asks Miles what happened at school Quint’s voice is heard. Miles shrieks and the candle goes out. Miles is tempted by Quint to pick up the letter. He steals it and rushes off. Miles distracts the grown-up’s attention by playing the piano, so they do not notice Flora going off to the lake. Mrs Grose and the Governess find Flora by the lake. The Governess tries to make Flora say that she can see Mrs Jessel, but she shouts that she can’t see anybody. Mrs Grose takes her home. In the last scene Flora has become mad. Mrs Grose tells the Governess that her letter to the uncle must have been stolen. She asks Miles whether he stole it. He denies it, but all the time he can see Peter Quint who is telling him he must not tell them the truth about him. In the end Miles screams: “Peter Quint! You devil!” and then dies. The Governess is left holding the dead boy in her arms. There are usually 13 players in the orchestra. The instruments used are: Two violins, viola, cello, double bass, flute/alto flute/piccolo, oboe/english horn, clarinet/bass clarinet, bassoon, horn, harp, piano/celesta and percussion.

The Tsar's Bride (Tsarskaya nevesta in Russian) is an opera by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. It was the tenth opera the composer wrote. The words (libretto) were written by Il’ya Tyumenev who based the story on a book called “The Tsar’s Bride" by Lev Mei. The opera was composed in 1898. The first performance took place in 1899 at the Moscow theater of the Private Opera of S.I. Mamontov. The story is supposed to take place in the autumn of 1572 in Moscow. At this time Russia was ruled by a very cruel tsar called Ivan the Terrible. Tsar Ivan had a group of people who guarded him. They were called oprichniki. The oprichniki were like bodyguards, but they were told to kill anybody who was not loyal to the tsar, so they behaved like terrorists, killing, raping and stealing wherever they went. In the opera there are also “Boyars”. A Boyar was a nobleman. Griaznoy is an oprichnik. Although he already has a lover, Lubasha, he now decides he loves Marfa, the daughter of the merchant Sobakin. Marfa is already engaged to be married to Lykov, a boyar. There is much merrymaking and singing at a feast. Then Griaznoy asks to be left alone with Bomelius, the tsar’s doctor. He asks him to get him a love potion. Lubasha, who is hiding, hears what he says and realizes that he does not love her any more. When the doctor goes, Griaznoy is horrible to Lubasha and tells her to go. She now wants to talk to Bomelius. A lot of people are coming out of church. They talk about the autumn weather, but when the oprichniki appear they are very frightened and start talking about whom the tsar is going to choose for his bride. Marfa talks to her friend Duniasha about how she has loved Lykov ever since they were children. Tsar Ivan passes by. She does not recognize him, but she is very frightened at the way the Tsar is staring at her. Sobakin comes in with Lykov and the four of them sing about looking forward to the wedding. Lyubasha now goes to Bomelius and asks for another magic potion which she wants to give to Griaznoi to stop him loving Marfa. Bomelius says he will give her the potion if she will make love to him. Lyubasha agrees and goes inside with him. At the wedding celebrations Sobakin tells Lykov that he will have to wait before his marriage to Marfa can be confirmed. The Tsar himself is looking for a girl to marry and has asked to see Sobakin’s daughters. Griaznoy realizes he needs to use the love potion quickly so he asks to be invited to the wedding. At the celebration he puts the potion in Marfa’s drink. A messenger comes with the news that the Tsar has chosen Marfa to be his wife. Everyone is horrified and Sobakin collapses. Sobakin is at the Tsar's palace. He is proud because his daughter is now the Tsarevna (the Tsar’s wife) and he himself has been made a Boyar. But he is also worried because Marfa has become very ill. Griaznoy comes in and greets Sobakin (who are now both boyars). He says that the person who poisoned Marfa has confessed. Marfa rushes in and tells Griaznoi to speak. He says that Lykov was tortured and then confessed to having poisoned Marfa. Lykov was then executed by Griaznoi himself. Marfa goes mad when she hears this. In her madness she thinks Griaznoy is Lykov. This eventually makes Griaznoy confess that he himself at put the potion into her drink. He did not realize it was poisonous. Lyubasha then confesses that she had put her potion in the place of Griaznoi’s potion. She blames Griaznoy and invites him to kill her. He kills her, then he is taken to prison to be executed. As he is taken away, Marfa, in her madness, once again mistakes Griaznoy for Lykov. She invites him to return the next day to visit her. Then she dies.

The Truth Is is the third studio album by English singer and songwriter Alexandra Burke. It was released on 16 March 2018 through Decca Records. It is Burke's first album since 2012's Heartbreak on Hold and her first album since leaving Syco.

The band formed in 2012 and signed to Mercury Records (now Virgin EMI Records) in the November of the same year. They have released five studio albums.
